overview.title: The three parts of the universal workflow, and starting 6.1 Defining the task
overview.chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning
overview.main_topic: The rest of the list of example ML projects, the three-part structure of the universal workflow (define the task, develop a model, deploy the model), and the opening questions of section 6.1 about understanding the context of a task
overview.central_idea: Real projects don't come with a keras.datasets dataset; a universal blueprint — define the task, develop a model, deploy the model — consolidates chapters 4 and 5. It starts with deeply understanding the customer's context: why they need it, how the model will be used, what data exists, and which ML task maps to the business problem.
overview.importance: This page is the table of contents of practical ML engineering. Every later chapter's projects implicitly follow these three phases, and the questions in 6.1 prevent the most expensive mistake: solving the wrong problem well.
learning_objectives: Recognize the variety of real problems the workflow must handle (recommendation, fraud, CTR, visual anomaly detection, remote sensing)
Describe the three parts of the workflow and the sub-steps of each
Explain how the 'develop a model' phase reuses chapter 5's fit-then-regularize procedure
List the context questions to ask before framing a problem
prerequisites: Chapter 5 summary (p.193–194): generalization, evaluation, fit then regularize

summary:
The page completes the list of hypothetical consulting projects begun on p.195: a **music recommendation** system for an online radio, **credit card fraud** detection for an e-commerce site, predicting **display ad click-through rate** to choose which ad to serve to a given user at a given time, flagging **anomalous cookies** on a manufacturing conveyor belt, and using **satellite images** to locate as-yet unknown **archaeological sites**.

It would be convenient to import the right dataset from `keras.datasets` and start fitting, but in reality "you'll have to start from scratch."

The chapter therefore presents a **universal step-by-step blueprint** for any ML problem, consolidating chapters 4 and 5 and giving context for the rest of the book. It has three parts:

1. **Define the task** — understand the problem domain and the business logic behind the request; collect a dataset; understand what the data represents; choose how to measure success.
2. **Develop a model** — prepare the data for a model; select an evaluation protocol and a simple baseline to beat; train a first model that has generalization power and can overfit; then regularize and tune until you get the best possible generalization.
3. **Deploy the model** — present your work to stakeholders; ship the model to a web server, mobile app, web page or embedded device; monitor its performance in the wild; start collecting the data for the next model generation.

**Section 6.1, Defining the task**, opens with a series of questions: Why is the customer trying to solve this problem? What value will they get? How will the model be used and fit into their business processes? What data is available or could be collected? What kind of ML task maps to the business problem?

**Section 6.1.1, Framing the problem**, begins: framing usually involves many detailed discussions with stakeholders, and a list of key questions follows on p.197.

paragraphs.excerpt: Building a music recommendation system for users of an online radio.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Five more projects arriving at the imagined consulting shop: music recommendation for an online radio; credit card fraud detection for an e-commerce site; predicting display ad click-through rate to pick which ad to serve a given user at a given time; flagging anomalous cookies on a cookie-production conveyor belt; finding unknown archaeological sites from satellite images.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The list is deliberately diverse: different data modalities (user behavior logs, transactions, ad impressions, camera images, satellite imagery), seemingly different task types, and very different data availability. As p.197 shows, the right ML framing is not always the obvious one (e.g. the 'anomalous cookies' project turns out to be binary classification, not an anomaly-detection technique). Together with the two projects of p.195, these seven examples are reused throughout section 6.1 to illustrate framing and data collection.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The point of a *universal* workflow is that it must handle all of these; keep them in mind as test cases while reading the steps.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: fraud and anomalous-cookie detection are classically imbalanced problems, which will matter for the choice of success metric (section 6.1.4, p.202).

paragraphs.what_it_says: Part 1: understand the domain and the business logic behind the request; collect a dataset; understand what the data represents; choose how to measure success.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Four sub-steps that map to sections 6.1.1 (framing), 6.1.2 (collecting a dataset), 6.1.3 (understanding your data) and 6.1.4 (choosing a measure of success).

paragraphs.what_it_says: Part 2: prepare data for the model; select an evaluation protocol and a simple baseline to beat; train a first model with generalization power that can overfit; then regularize and tune until you get the best generalization.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Part 3: present your work to stakeholders; ship the model to a web server, mobile app, web page or embedded device; monitor performance in the wild; start collecting the data needed for the next model generation.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Deployment is not the end: real-world data drifts, so monitoring and continual data collection make the workflow a loop rather than a line.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Many projects fail after a technically good model is built — through unmet expectations or silent degradation in production.

paragraphs.excerpt: You can’t do good work without a deep understanding of the context
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 6.1 opens: good work requires deep understanding of the context. Questions to ask: Why is the customer trying to solve this problem? What value will they derive? How will the model be used? How will it fit into their business processes? What data is available or could be collected? What ML task can be mapped to the business problem?
paragraphs.what_it_means: These questions translate a business request into ML terms. 'How will the model be used' determines latency, cost and error trade-offs; 'what data is available' determines feasibility; 'what ML task' determines inputs, targets and loss.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: They are the antidote to building an impressive model nobody can use.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book, example: for CTR prediction, 'how will the model be used' (ranking ads in milliseconds) implies a lightweight model and a calibrated probability output.

terminology.meaning: Anyone with an interest in the project's outcome: customer, users, domain experts, engineers.

connections: p.623: understanding the problem domain is a prerequisite for any successful application of ML

concepts.name: Universal workflow of machine learning
concepts.definition: A three-part blueprint for any ML project: define the task, develop a model, deploy the model.
concepts.intuition: Problem → data and metric → model → production → new data → better model.
concepts.technical: Define: domain/business logic, dataset, data understanding, success metric. Develop: data prep, evaluation protocol, baseline, model that overfits, regularize/tune. Deploy: stakeholders, shipping, monitoring, collecting data for the next generation.
concepts.significance: Consolidates chapters 4–5 and frames all later chapters.
concepts.example: Cookie flagging: install cameras, label images, choose a metric, train a convnet, deploy on the production line, monitor.
concepts.misconception: That the workflow ends when the model is deployed.

concepts.name: Problem framing
concepts.definition: Translating a business request into a precise ML problem: what data, what target, what task type, what constraints.
concepts.intuition: Turning 'find fraud' into 'predict P(fraud | transaction features)'.
concepts.technical: Driven by the context questions of 6.1 and the stakeholder discussions of 6.1.1.
concepts.significance: Errors here propagate to everything downstream.
concepts.example: Spam/offensive flagging framed as 3-class text classification (spam, offensive, acceptable — see p.199).
concepts.misconception: That framing is obvious from the request.

concepts.name: Baseline to beat
concepts.definition: A simple reference performance a model must exceed to demonstrate it has learned anything.
concepts.intuition: If you can't beat guessing, nothing else matters.
concepts.technical: Part of the 'develop a model' phase; called achieving statistical power (p.205).
concepts.example: Majority-class accuracy on an imbalanced fraud dataset.
concepts.misconception: That high accuracy alone means the model is useful (it may only equal the baseline).

deeper.title: Framing the seven projects (a preview exercise)
deeper.body:
Beyond the book — one possible framing for each project, to compare against what section 6.1 says later:

| Project | Input | Target | Task type |
|---|---|---|---|
| Photo search | image | set of concept tags | multilabel classification |
| Spam/offensive flagging | post text | spam / offensive / acceptable | multiclass classification |
| Music recommendation | user history + track | will the user like it? | ranking / recommendation |
| Credit card fraud | transaction | fraud or not | binary classification (imbalanced) |
| Ad CTR | user, ad, context | click probability | probability estimation |
| Cookie flagging | conveyor image | normal / anomalous | binary classification or anomaly detection |
| Archaeology | satellite tile | site present? | image classification / detection |

The book's own answers on p.197 differ for several of these, which makes for a useful comparison: music recommendation is better handled by matrix factorization (collaborative filtering) rather than deep learning; CTR is framed as scalar regression; cookie flagging is binary classification preceded by an object-detection crop stage, with the book explicitly saying anomaly-detection techniques would *not* be a good fit; and the archaeology project is an image similarity ranking task.

deeper.title: Why the workflow is a loop
deeper.body: The last item of 'Deploy the model' — start collecting the data you'll need for the next model generation — feeds back into 'Define the task / collect a dataset'. Beyond the book: production data reveals cases the original dataset missed (concept drift, new user behaviors), so each deployed model generates the training data for its successor.

visualizations.why: The three bullets on this page define the workflow and its sub-steps; the final sub-step loops back to data collection.

misconceptions.claim: You can usually start by importing a dataset and training a model.
misconceptions.correction: In the real world you start from scratch: from a problem, then data collection and framing.

misconceptions.claim: Model development is where most of the important decisions are made.
misconceptions.correction: Defining the task (domain, data, metric) and deployment (expectations, monitoring) are equally decisive.
Deployment includes monitoring and collecting data for the next model generation — the workflow repeats.

takeaways: Real projects are diverse (recommendation, fraud, CTR, visual anomaly detection, remote sensing) and don't come with a ready dataset.
The universal workflow has three parts: define the task, develop a model, deploy the model.
Developing a model reuses chapter 5: baseline, model that can overfit, then regularize and tune.
Deployment includes stakeholder communication, shipping, monitoring, and collecting data for the next model generation.
Defining the task starts with questions about why, value, usage, business processes, available data, and the matching ML task.

questions.question: Which of these is part of the 'Develop a model' phase as described on this page?
options: Monitoring the model's performance in the wild
Selecting a model evaluation protocol and a simple baseline to beat
Understanding the business logic underlying the customer's request
questions.answer: Selecting a model evaluation protocol and a simple baseline to beat
questions.explanation: That item is in the 'Develop a model' bullet. Monitoring and presenting belong to 'Deploy the model'; business logic belongs to 'Define the task'.

questions.question: Name the four sub-steps of 'Define the task'.
questions.answer: Understand the problem domain and business logic; collect a dataset; understand what the data represents; choose how to measure success.
questions.explanation: From the first workflow bullet; they correspond to sections 6.1.1–6.1.4.

questions.question: Why does the 'Deploy the model' phase end with collecting data for the next model generation, and what does that imply about the workflow's shape?
questions.answer: Because deployed models encounter new and changing real-world data; collecting it lets you build an improved successor. The workflow is therefore a loop, not a one-way pipeline.
questions.explanation: The bullet lists this as the last deployment step; section 6.3.4 (p.212) covers maintaining your model.

questions.question: Which question is NOT among those listed at the start of section 6.1?
options: What value will they derive from the solution?
How will it fit into your customer's business processes?
What kind of machine learning task can be mapped to the business problem?
questions.explanation: Optimizer choice is a model-development detail; the other three are verbatim context questions of section 6.1.

questions.question: How does 'Develop a model' relate to the summary of chapter 5?
questions.answer: It reuses chapter 5's procedure: pick an evaluation protocol, beat a baseline, train a model that has generalization power and can overfit, then regularize and tune for the best generalization.
questions.explanation: The page says the template consolidates chapters 4 and 5; compare p.194.

questions.question: Pick the credit card fraud project. Which of the section 6.1 questions do you think most changes how you'd build the model, and why?
questions.answer: Example answer: 'How will your model be used?' — if it blocks transactions in real time, false positives annoy customers and latency limits are strict; if it only flags for human review, recall matters more and latency less. This affects the metric, threshold and model size.
questions.explanation: Open-ended; tests understanding of why context questions drive technical choices.

questions.question: Can you recite the three parts of the workflow and two sub-steps of each without looking?
questions.answer: Define the task (e.g. collect a dataset, choose a success metric); Develop a model (e.g. beat a baseline, regularize and tune); Deploy the model (e.g. ship it, monitor it).
